segments.say: Waiting is not going away. No matter how fast technology becomes, no matter how efficient our lives are, there will always be waiting. Waiting for people, for news, for seasons to change, for wounds to heal, for children to grow, for dreams to come true. So perhaps the question isn't how to avoid waiting. But how to wait well.

Think of a gardener. A gardener plants a seed, and then waits. There's no way to rush it. You can water it, give it light, protect it from frost. But you can't pull the plant up to make it grow faster. A good gardener learns to be patient. To do what can be done, and then to let time do its work.

show.cap: Some things can only grow slowly

segments.say: So let's gather what we've learned into a few gentle practices. The first is to fill the time. Remember the airport. Occupied time feels shorter than empty time. When you know you'll be waiting, bring something with you. A book, a puzzle, a podcast, a notebook. Or simply plan to notice the world around you. A wait with something in it is a lighter wait.

The second is to create certainty where you can. Uncertainty is often the heaviest part of waiting. Ask for an estimate. Check the tracking. Decide when you'll next check for news, instead of checking all the time. And for others, give updates. A small piece of certainty can turn an anxious wait into a calm one.

show.cap: Two. Create certainty where you can.

segments.say: The third is to find your flow. For the long, important waits, like waiting for results, plan activities that can truly absorb you. Not just distractions, but things that are challenging enough to fill your mind. Cooking, music, sport, a craft, a puzzle. Flow doesn't make the news come sooner. But it can make the wait far kinder.

The fourth is to look back, not just ahead. In a line, the people behind you can lift your mood. In life, remembering how far you've already come can do the same. When the wait feels long, take a moment to notice the progress you've already made. The steps behind you are real too.

show.cap: Four. Look back, not just ahead.

segments.say: The fifth is to savor what's coming. When you're waiting for something good, don't rush through the anticipation. Let it be part of the pleasure. Like tea that needs a few minutes to steep, some things are better for the waiting. The days before a holiday, the evening before seeing a friend, these are gifts in themselves.

show.cap: Some things are better for the waiting

segments.say: The sixth is to shorten the dread. When something unpleasant is ahead, and you have a choice, consider getting it over with sooner. Make the call this morning. Book the earliest appointment. And when you can't shorten it, gently move your attention elsewhere. The shadow of a thing is usually bigger than the thing itself.

The seventh is to wait together, when you can. Solo waits feel longer than shared ones. If you're waiting for something difficult, tell someone. Let them keep you company, even just with a message now and then. And when someone you know is waiting, offer to wait with them. Shared waiting is lighter waiting.

The eighth is about being someone others can wait for. Remember the children and the reliable adult. When we keep our promises, show up on time, and come back when we say we will, we help the people around us learn that waiting is worth it. Reliability is a quiet gift of patience to others.

The ninth is to make the patient choice easy. Our present selves are often impatient. So help them. Decide in advance, set up automatic habits, remove temptations. Put the marshmallow out of sight, so to speak. It's not about willpower. It's about kind and clever design for your own life.

show.cap: Nine. Make the patient choice easy.

segments.say: And the tenth is to know when to stop waiting. Not every wait is worth it. Sometimes we stay in a line, or a situation, out of habit, or because we've already waited so long. It's okay to step out. Patience is a virtue, but so is knowing when to choose something else.

show.cap: Ten. Know when to stop waiting.

segments.say: I also want to suggest a gentler way of seeing waiting altogether. We often think of waiting as time stolen from our lives. A pause before real life resumes. But waiting is life too. The minutes at the bus stop, the evening before the big day, the season before the harvest. They're part of the story, not a gap in it.

So here's the art of waiting well, in short. Fill the time. Create certainty where you can. Find your flow for the big waits. Look back at how far you've come. Savor what's coming. Shorten the dread. Wait together. Be reliable for others. Make patience easy. And know when it's time to stop waiting.

We're nearing the end of our journey now. Before we start to slow down for the night, let's take a final look back at everything we've discovered about waiting, and choose a few simple ideas to carry into tomorrow.
